conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m a clinician who specializes in looking after moms’ emotional well-being in the weeks and months after having a baby. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the EPDS (the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). Its purpose is simply to help us understand how you’ve been feeling lately, so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything we discuss stays confidential, and this room is a judgment-free zone. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions that ask about the past seven days; there are no “right” answers—just whatever feels true for you today. When we’re finished, I’ll share what the results mean and we can talk about next steps together.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?
I’ve actually been able to laugh—like, my husband made a silly joke about dirty-diaper explosions yesterday and I cracked up. It hasn’t felt hard to find things funny this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
As much as I always could.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yes, I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or taking her for a walk in the stroller. I wouldn’t say I’m bouncing with excitement, but I do enjoy those moments.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If she spits up right after I’ve changed her, I might think “should’ve waited,” but I don’t dwell on it. I know babies are messy and it’s not my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I catch myself worrying that she’s breathing okay when she’s sleeping, but it’s usually just a quick check and I’m fine. It’s not constant or overwhelming—more like a little “mom radar” that pops up and then fades.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden panic. I get a little startled when she cries out of nowhere, but it passes right away.
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes, yeah—like when she cluster-feeds and I can’t even get a shower in. For a minute it feels like the to-do list is swallowing me, but once she naps I reset and it’s manageable again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s been okay—when she lets me have it. I’m tired, but once I’m in bed I drift off pretty easily.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable. I get a little emotional when I’m extra tired, but it’s not the same as feeling down or blue.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had any of those “can’t-stop” crying spells. My eyes might water when I’m really tired, but it’s not from feeling unhappy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression Screening Summary (Edinburgh Scale self-report)

Positive indicators  
- Occasional situational “getting on top of me” when infant cluster-feeds; resolves after brief respite.  
- Transient, non-clinical worry about infant breathing during sleep.

Absent indicators  
- No sustained low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, panic, sleep–mood linkage, crying spells, or self-harm ideation.

Pattern  
- Overall affective stability; stressors framed as normative new-mother challenges with rapid return to baseline.

Screening impression  
- Current responses do not suggest elevated risk for postpartum depression or anxiety; no safety concerns identified.
